messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao presents as a 46-year-old man whose stoic demeanor seems to barely contain a profound and restless agitation. A firefighter with two decades of service, he describes the last eighteen months as a "slow-motion collapse" following his volunteer deployment as a relief worker in a war-torn region. It was there, amidst the rubble of a besieged city, that the event occurred. His unit was evacuating a partially collapsed apartment building when the sounds began—shrieks from an adjacent, inaccessible wing of the complex. They were under strict orders to hold their position. Bao remembers the commander’s voice on the radio, sharp and absolute, but it’s drowned out by the memory of the screams, which were not of pain, but of a particular kind of terror. Then, a deafening blast threw him against a wall. The world dissolved into dust and a searing, white-hot agony in his back and left leg.

The memories of that day do not return to him as a story. Instead, they come in jagged pieces, a sequence he can never seem to straighten out. Sometimes it's just the sound of the screams, other times it's the physical sensation of the impact, a phantom pain that shoots down his spine so intensely he has to brace himself against a wall. When he tries to explain it, the words fail him. He knows what he wants to say, the horror he wants to convey, but the vocabulary evaporates, leaving him with a frustrating, inarticulate silence. He has come to believe that the chaos of the event permanently scrambled his ability to make sense of it, not just for others, but for himself.

Back at his firehouse in the States, the familiar environment has become a landscape of hidden threats. The long, tense quiet in the truck on the way to a call feels menacing, a silence he is certain is about to be shattered by catastrophe. A car backfiring on the street, or the sudden whoosh and bang of a backdraft at a scene, can instantly transport him back to the explosion. In those moments, he feels the shrapnel in his back all over again. His crew, once his brothers, now give him a wide berth. His irritability has grown into a constant, simmering anger that boils over without warning, and his captain has formally warned him about his aggressive outbursts. He feels their distance as a judgment, confirming a belief that has taken root deep inside him: he no longer belongs anywhere. He is not one of them anymore.

At home in his empty apartment, the one he moved into after his wife left, he is haunted. A news report mentioning sexual violence will trigger the memory of the screams from the apartment wing, and with it, a wave of guilt so powerful it feels like a physical illness. He is certain he acted in a way that goes against everything he is supposed to be—a protector, a rescuer. He should have disobeyed orders. He should have done *something*. This thought loops endlessly, a self-inflicted torment. To manage these overwhelming feelings, he has developed his own painful rituals. He tries to forcefully suppress the thoughts, pushing them down until the pressure is unbearable. When that fails, he will dig his fingernails into the flesh of his arm, the sharp, grounding pain a temporary release from the emotional agony. Before every shift, he performs a sequence of silent actions—tapping his helmet three times, checking the latch on his door twice—a desperate, magical attempt to ensure nothing bad will happen to his crew, a responsibility he feels he catastrophically failed once before.

Bao sought therapy after his captain put him on administrative leave, telling him he couldn’t return to active duty until he was “cleared.” The ultimatum was both a humiliation and a lifeline. He feels his life has been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma, a permanent stain on his character. What frightens him most is the conviction that the man he was—the confident firefighter, the husband, the man who believed in his own moral courage—is gone forever, replaced by this angry, frightened stranger.
